title: Japan Defense Minister Visits Yasukuni Shrine as Nation Marks 81st WWII Surrender Anniversary
excerpt: Shinjiro Koizumi's visit to the war-linked shrine drew criticism from China and South Korea, as Prime Minister Takaichi sent a ritual offering.
body:
• Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited Yasukuni Shrine on August 15, the 81st anniversary of Japan's WWII surrender
  • Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual offering to the shrine, which honors 2.5 million war dead including 14 Class-A war criminals
  • China and South Korea have condemned visits by senior Japanese officials as glossing over wartime aggression
  • No sitting Japanese prime minister has visited the shrine since Shinzo Abe in 2013

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited the Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo on Saturday as Japan marked the 81st anniversary of its surrender in World War Two, a move certain to strain relations with Asian neighbors who view the shrine as a symbol of wartime aggression.

Koizumi, the son of former Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi, wore a dark suit and tie as he paid his respects at the shrine, local media images showed, according to Reuters. He has visited Yasukuni in the past, including as agriculture minister last year.

A Shrine That Divides

Yasukuni commemorates roughly 2.5 million of Japan's war dead. Among them are 14 wartime leaders convicted of the most serious war crimes by Allied tribunals after Japan's 1945 defeat, along with more than 1,000 others found guilty of lesser offenses. Japanese officials have framed past visits as personal acts to honor those who died in the nation's wars.

Kimi Onoda, Japan's minister for economic security, also visited on Saturday, public broadcaster NHK reported. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who took office last October, did not visit in person but sent a ritual offering to the shrine, according to Kyodo news agency.

"China strongly opposes the Japanese Defense Minister's visit to Yasukuni Shrine, and urges the Japanese side to reflect on its history of aggression."

— Senior Colonel Wu Qian, Chinese Ministry of National Defense

Diplomatic Flashpoint

China and South Korea have consistently criticized visits by senior Japanese officials to Yasukuni, saying they whitewash Tokyo's wartime actions and damage diplomatic ties. Beijing has called the shrine "a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism" that honors those "directly responsible for past aggression."

The last sitting Japanese prime minister to visit Yasukuni was Shinzo Abe in December 2013, a trip that drew an expression of disappointment from the Obama administration. The last premier to visit on the anniversary of Japan's surrender was the elder Koizumi, in 2006.

Broader Regional Tensions

The visit comes against a backdrop of heightened military activity in the region. Earlier this year, Takaichi's government revised Japan's arms export rules to allow the overseas sale of weapons with lethal capabilities, and signed a deal worth approximately $6.5 billion to supply Australia with warships. China condemned both moves alongside Takaichi's spring ritual offering to Yasukuni.

Beijing's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun challenged Tokyo in April, asking how Japan could "profess itself as a peace-loving country" while simultaneously increasing its military budget, deploying offensive missiles, relaxing weapons export restrictions, and sending offerings to Yasukuni.

Domestic Divisions

Within Japan, the shrine remains contentious. Tens of thousands of protesters gathered near the National Diet earlier this year to defend Article 9 of the Constitution, Japan's pacifist clause, chanting "No to war" and "Do not undermine Article 9."

Many Japanese citizens visit Yasukuni to pay respects to relatives who died in the wars. Conservative politicians maintain that leaders should be able to commemorate the war dead without apology. But regional neighbors continue to view official visits as an affront — a tension that shows no signs of easing on the 81st anniversary of a conflict that reshaped East Asia.
